items.title: Nanotoxicity and nanogenotoxicity in cancer therapy mechanisms dual roles and emerging mitigation strategies
items.abstract: Nanomedicine has emerged as a transformative strategy in cancer therapy, enabling precision drug delivery, improved therapeutic efficacy, and personalized treatment paradigms. Despite these advances, clinical translation remains constrained by unresolved nanotoxicity concerns. This minireview critically examines the mechanistic basis of nanoparticle-induced toxicity in oncology, with a particular focus on oxidative stress arising from lysosomal membrane permeabilization, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cytoplasmic redox enzyme dysregulation, which collectively disrupt cellular redox homeostasis and drive excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. Key ROS-amplifying pathways, including NADPH oxidase activation, redox-sensitive signalling cascades, and Fenton-like reactions associated with metal-based nanoparticles, are highlighted as central mediators of cellular injury. Immune activation and signaling pathway perturbations are discussed in the context of chronic inflammation and altered tumor–immune interactions. The review further addresses nano-genotoxicity as a critical safety endpoint, encompassing DNA strand breaks, chromosomal instability, epigenetic reprogramming, and persistent gene expression alterations. The dualistic nature of nanomedicine is illustrated using representative nanomaterials, including carbon nanotubes (CNTs), which exhibit high drug-loading capacity alongside documented genotoxic and oxidative liabilities, and cerium oxide nanoparticles, whose antioxidant or cytotoxic behavior is dictated by physicochemical properties and intracellular context. Strategies to mitigate nanotoxicity are discussed, including surface functionalization, biocompatible coatings, biodegradable nanocarriers, and mechanism-informed toxicity screening approaches aligned with regulatory expectations. Finally, emerging directions are outlined, emphasizing artificial intelligence–assisted nanotoxicity prediction, computational modeling of nano–bio interactions, standardized safety assessment frameworks, and interdisciplinary collaboration as critical enablers of safe clinical translation. These insights support the rational design of safer nanomedicines and reinforce the need for mechanistic toxicology to guide their development for cancer care.

items.title: Navigating the double-edged sword: an integrated TAM–SET model for sustainable knowledge sharing in the AI era
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address the paradox where artificial intelligence (AI) enhances knowledge sharing efficiency but may erode user motivation. It develops and tests an integrated model synthesizing the technology acceptance model (TAM) and social exchange theory (SET) to explain the context-dependent drivers of sustainable knowledge sharing in the AI era. Design/methodology/approach A survey-based empirical design is employed. Data from 201 respondents were collected and analyzed using path analysis across three AI-related knowledge-sharing scenarios to examine the relationships among perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived benefits, perceived costs, sharing intention and knowledge-sharing behavior. Findings While perceived benefits and ease of use are stable drivers of sharing intention, the role of perceived cost is dynamic. It acts as a deterrent in direct human-AI interaction but transforms into a ‘sunk cost investment’ that promotes sharing in interpersonal contexts. A significant “intention-behavior” gap is also identified, stemming from poor technological affordances. Practical implications Actionable guidance is provided for platform designers and managers. Designers should create low-friction contribution channels and leverage “sunk cost” psychology. Managers should adopt context-specific incentive strategies and prioritize system usability to foster a sustainable knowledge ecosystem. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is one of the first studies to empirically model the sustainability paradox of AI-driven knowledge sharing. It advances theory by demonstrating the context-dependent role of core constructs like “perceived cost,” extending TAM and SET to the human–AI collaboration domain.
